title: Remembering Everything

post.author: u/counter_hand_snezana
post.title: I work nights on the counter at a 24-hour tool-hire depot. At 04:48 a contractor asked our assistant about a saw, and it answered from the cement mixer's manual, with a score of 0.91.

blocks.text: I'm Snezana, night counter hand at a 24-hour tool-hire depot. Builders hire our saws, mixers and generators, and the first vans collect at 05:00.

On the counter sits the assistant: a program, a set of instructions a computer follows, that answers questions typed in plain words. It answers from our 3,000 pages of tool manuals. Head office cut those pages into 12,000 pieces, four to a page. Each piece is a chunk.

A computer can't tell what a chunk means. So another program, the embedding model, turns each chunk into a list of numbers, like map co-ordinates for its meaning. Chunks about similar things get nearby numbers. That list is the chunk's embedding.
All 12,000 lists, each kept with its chunk, make up the index: like the index at the back of a book, but by meaning. It lives on a computer in the locked yard office across the yard.

A question goes through it in steps. First, the same embedding model turns my question into numbers. Then the index finds the chunks whose numbers sit closest. Then it hands those chunks to the language model, the program that writes the answer from them. Look it up, then answer: head office calls that RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation.
How close two lists sit is a score from 0 to 1, called similarity. Only chunks above 0.80 are handed over: that's the match bar. Every answer shows its source page and its similarity.

Since launch in March 2025 there had been one embedding model, v1. The provider, the company that runs it, retires v1 at the end of Wednesday 30 September. Its new model, v2, makes lists of the same length, so nothing complains if the two are mixed.

Haverly at head office got the provider's notice and picked quiet hours. At 00:00 a job, a program that runs on its own, began re-indexing: making every chunk's numbers again with v2. Its steps: take the next chunk by number, send it to v2, write the new numbers over the old. 1,500 chunks an hour, done by 08:00. At 00:00 it moved questions to v2 as well, to match the new numbers.

At 04:48 Grzegorz, a groundworker, asked me for the fuel mix of our item C-27, a petrol cut-off saw. I typed it in and read the answer aloud. It was the drum speed of M-06, our cement mixer. He laughed. Then he saw the similarity, 0.91, and stopped.
Haverly sent me the screen's full list this morning. Each line shows a chunk's number, its manual page and its similarity to the question; the last line is the job's progress.

04:48:12  question: fuel mix, C-27 cut-off saw
chunk 11,208  M-06 cement mixer p6, drum speed   0.91  handed over
chunk  2,415  G-41 generator p3, fuel tank        0.74
chunk  5,030  T-33 hedge trimmer p2, fuel cap     0.69
chunk  9,612  C-27 cut-off saw p4, fuel           0.42
job: 7,200 of 12,000 chunks done, in order from chunk 1
The saw's own page scored 0.42. The mixer had never been near a saw.

The re-index job has not started until 00:00, then runs, amber, all the rest of the window. The saw's chunk 9,612 and the mixer's chunk 11,208 are green until 00:00 and then still v1 for the rest of the window. Markers: 00:00 the job starts, 04:48 the mixer page scores 0.91.

From 00:00 the job re-made chunks with v2 in chunk order, 1,500 an hour, and questions moved to v2 at once (red). By 04:48 it had done chunks 1 to 7,200, so the saw's chunk 9,612 and the mixer's 11,208 still held v1 numbers when the mixer page scored 0.91 against a question about the saw.

blocks.text: I found C-27's paper manual on the back shelf, and he left at 05:05. The job finished at 08:00, and Haverly says every answer since looks right. But one day v2 will retire too. What should head office change before the next model?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two counts, then a question. At 04:48, how many chunks held numbers made by v2, and how many still held v1's? Which model turned Grzegorz's question into numbers? Now read the chunk numbers on Haverly's list: which of them had the job reached? Two embedding models are like two mapmakers who each drew their own grid: the same co-ordinates point to different places on each map. So what was 0.91 measuring?

replies.author: u/counter_hand_snezana
replies.text: 7,200 on v2 and 4,800 still on v1. v2 made the question's numbers. The job had reached chunks 2,415 and 5,030, the generator and the trimmer, but not 9,612 or 11,208. The saw and the mixer still had v1's numbers.

comments.author: u/high_bar_dragica
comments.text: 0.91 is a strong score, so your bar is the problem, not the model. Raise it to 0.95 and junk can't get through: a mixer page will never clear 0.95 on a saw question. It's one setting, no rebuild, and head office could change it tonight.

replies.author: u/counter_hand_snezana
replies.text: Haverly says the bar has been 0.80 since launch.

comments.author: u/small_cuts_aoibheann
comments.text: A quarter of a page is too big. A chunk that size holds several facts, so its numbers are a blur of all of them. Cut the manuals smaller, one fact to a chunk, and each chunk's numbers sit right on top of the question it answers.

reply.prompt: Head office meets on Thursday 1 October. What should they change before the next model change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Build the new index beside the old one, and switch questions only when it is done.
options.part2: On Thursday 1 October head office agreed, and Haverly wrote the plan down. Every chunk now carries the name of the model that made its numbers, and the search refuses to compare a question with a chunk from another model. The next move builds a second index beside the first while questions stay on the old model and the old index. When the new index is complete, a test set of five known questions, each with the page that should answer it, runs against it. Only when all five find their right page do questions and index switch together, in one step. In the sim, replaying 30 September that way: questions stay on v1 all night, and at 04:48 the C-27 question finds the saw's own fuel page at 0.88. The new index reaches 12,000 chunks at 08:00, the test set finds 5 of 5, and questions and index switch together at 08:00. Snezana reads Grzegorz the right page.
options.senior: An index is a second copy of your documents, written in one model's numbers, and it has to move with that model. Build the new index beside the old one and keep questions on the old model until the new index is complete. Then test it with known questions whose right pages you already know, and switch questions and index together in one step. Store the model's name with every chunk, and have the search refuse any comparison across models, so a mix-up fails loudly instead of answering with confidence. It costs room for two indexes for a night, and a test set someone must keep up to date.

options.text: Raise the match bar from 0.80 to 0.95, so only very close chunks are handed over.
options.verdict: A higher bar over unlike numbers
options.part2: On Thursday 1 October head office raised the match bar to 0.95. In the sim, replaying 30 September in place with the bar at 0.95: at 04:48 the mixer's 0.91 is refused, and the C-27 question gets no match. But at 04:48 the test set's hedge trimmer question gets chunk 9,880, the saw's carry case page, at 0.97: a wrong page above even the higher bar. And after 08:00, with every chunk on v2, the saw's own page scores 0.89 and is refused too: 0 of 5 test questions find their right page. By the weekend the staff had stopped asking the assistant anything.
options.senior: A similarity score only means something when both lists were made by the same model. Between two models a score is chance, and chance can land anywhere, above 0.95 included. Raising the bar refuses some wrong pages and many right ones: on one model, the right pages in this sample score 0.84 to 0.89. Tune the bar on one model, with a test set; never use it to paper over a mix of two.

options.text: Take the assistant offline until every chunk has been made again with the new model.
options.part2: Head office agreed: for the next model change, the assistant goes offline for the whole re-index. In the sim, replaying 30 September that way: no answers from 00:00 to 08:00, 8 hours, then every answer right on v2. At 04:48 Grzegorz's question gets 'assistant offline', and Snezana goes to the back shelf for the paper manual, as she did that night. With the first vans at 05:00, every early question on a re-index night is answered by hand.
options.senior: Taking the assistant offline is honest: it never answers from mixed numbers. But it trades wrong answers for no answers for as long as the job runs: 8 hours here, longer as the manuals grow, and every model change repeats it. Building beside gives the same safety with no dark hours, at the cost of room for two indexes for a night. Offline is a fair fallback where there truly is no room for two.

options.text: Cut the manuals into smaller chunks, so that each one matches a question more closely.
options.verdict: Twice the chunks, twice the mixed hours
options.part2: Head office cut the manuals smaller: 24,000 chunks of about an eighth of a page. In the sim, replaying 30 September with half-size chunks: the job takes 16 hours, until 16:00, and every chunk number doubles, so at 04:48 7,200 chunks are on v2 and 16,800 still on v1. The saw's page and the mixer's are still v1, and the C-27 question still gets the mixer's drum speed at 0.91. At 08:00, 12,000 are on v2 and 12,000 on v1, and the wrong answer is still there.
options.senior: Chunk size changes what each list of numbers describes, and it is worth tuning with a test set. It does nothing about which model made the numbers. Twice the chunks is twice the re-index time at the same rate, so the mixed hours grow from 8 to 16. Smaller pieces also lose context: a page split from its heading can answer half a question.

sim.title: Replay the night of 30 September
sim.lede: You're Haverly at head office, replaying the night of Tuesday 29 to Wednesday 30 September 2026 from 23:48. As given data: 3,000 pages cut into 12,000 chunks, four to a page, numbered in the order their manuals were added. Until 00:00 every chunk and every question is turned into numbers by v1. At 00:00 a job re-makes chunks with v2 in chunk-number order, 1,500 an hour, 300 every 12-minute step, so all 12,000 are done at 08:00. The match bar is 0.80: only chunks scoring above it are handed over, and the highest is the answer's source. The test set is five known questions, the C-27 question first, each with its right page and one other page; the C-27 question has three others. Each sample chunk's similarity is given three ways: a v1 question against v1 numbers, a v2 question against v2 numbers, and a v2 question against v1 numbers, which is chance. In place, questions switch to v2 at 00:00 and meet whatever numbers each chunk holds. Beside, questions stay on v1 and the old index while a new v2 index is built, and switch with it only when the test set finds all 5 right pages. Half-size chunks make 24,000 chunks and double every chunk number; the sample keeps its scores. Offline turns the assistant off until the job is done. The version check refuses any chunk whose numbers came from a different model than the question's. Step the night in 12-minute steps.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step to 00:00. Questions move to v2 before any chunk is redone, and the C-27 question already gets the mixer at 0.91. Step on to 04:48: 7,200 on v2, 4,800 on v1, the mixer at 0.91 and 2 of 5 test questions right. Step to 06:36: the saw's chunk is redone, and the mixer still wins until 07:36. Play to 08:00: all on v2, the saw's page at 0.89, 5 of 5. Switch to building beside: the saw's page at 0.88 all night, and the switch at 08:00 after 5 of 5. Turn on the version check in place: at 04:48 no answer instead of a wrong one, 3 of 5 right and none wrong. Raise the bar to 0.95: the mixer is refused, but the trimmer question gets the saw's carry case at 0.97, and after 08:00 nothing passes. Try half-size chunks: 16 hours, the mixer still there at 08:00. Try offline: 8 hours with no answers.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the depot broke. At 00:00 a job began re-making the 12,000 chunks' numbers with v2, in place, and questions moved to v2 at the same moment; by 04:48 7,200 chunks held v2 numbers and 4,800 still held v1's, the saw's page and the mixer's among them, so a v2 question was measured against v1 numbers and the mixer's 0.91 was chance.

steps.title: Look it up, then answer: RAG, step by step.
steps.text: RAG has two halves. Building the index, in steps. First, cut the manuals into chunks; this is chunking, and what can go wrong is a cut through the middle of a table that splits one fact in two (LATENT's a3e02, Cutting the Pages, goes deep on this). Second, the embedding model turns each chunk into its embedding; what can go wrong is that the model changes, as it did tonight. Third, store each embedding with its chunk in a store built to find the closest lists of numbers quickly, called a vector database; what can go wrong is that it forgets which model made each list. Answering, in steps. First, the same model turns the question into numbers. Second, the vector database finds the closest chunks and keeps those above the match bar. Third, the language model writes the answer from the chunks it is handed; what can go wrong is that it can only be as right as those chunks. The Word Index kept a list from each word to the pages that hold it; this index is kept by meaning instead. LATENT's a3e01, Asking the Archive, and a3e03, The Vault of Vectors, teach these steps in full.

steps.title: Two models, two maps: why 0.91 meant nothing.
steps.text: An embedding is a position on one model's map. v1 and v2 each drew their own map, so the same numbers point to different places on each. Comparing a v2 question with a v1 chunk is reading one map's co-ordinates on the other, and the score that comes out is chance. Most chance scores are low, like the saw page's 0.42; some land high by luck, like the mixer's 0.91. Nothing complained, because both models make lists of the same length, and a length check is all the database can do. The job went in chunk order at 1,500 an hour: at 04:48, 4.8 hours in, it had done chunks 1 to 7,200. The generator's and trimmer's chunks, 2,415 and 5,030, held v2 numbers and scored honestly, 0.74 and 0.69, below the bar. The saw's 9,612 and the mixer's 11,208 still held v1's. Even after the saw's chunk was redone, the mixer's chance score beat its 0.89 until the mixer's chunk was redone too. Why never before: since launch in March 2025, 18 months, there was one model, so every comparison was on one map. Tonight's re-index was the first time two maps met. LATENT's a6e09, The Night It Changed Its Mind, covers a model changing under you; a3e07, When Retrieval Lies, covers confident wrong pages.

steps.title: The index is a second store that must move with its model.
steps.text: The manuals' text is the first store. The index is a second one, written in one model's numbers, and the two must change together. A re-index done safely, in steps. First, build a new index beside the old one, making every chunk's numbers with v2, while questions stay on v1 and the old index; what can go wrong is time and room: 8 hours here, and space for two indexes. Second, test it: run a test set, known questions whose right pages you already know, against the new index; what can go wrong is a test set too small or too old to notice a bad index (LATENT's a5e02, The Retrieval Scorecard, is how to score one). Third, switch questions and index together, in one step; what can go wrong is switching one without the other, which is exactly tonight. Through all of it, store the model's name with every chunk, so the search can refuse to compare across models. In the sim, built beside, questions get the saw's page all night, the test set finds 5 of 5 at 08:00, and the switch happens then. The Long Move uses the same idea, build beside and then switch, for a payment system.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: A 0.95 bar still compares unlike numbers. At 04:48 it refuses the mixer's 0.91, but the trimmer test question gets the saw's carry case at 0.97, and after 08:00 it refuses the saw's own 0.89, so 0 of 5 test questions pass. Smaller chunks double the job to 24,000 chunks and 16 hours, and the mixer still wins at 04:48 and at 08:00. Offline is never wrong, but it means 8 hours with no answers, right through the 05:00 vans. A bigger language model only reads what it is handed: given the mixer's page as the best match, the most it can do is say it doesn't know, and a confident page above the bar looks like an answer to any model. LATENT's a3e09, Keeping It Fresh, is about keeping an index up to date as pages change; this case is about moving the whole index when its model changes.

steps.title: The walk to the yard office.
steps.text: At 05:12, with Grzegorz gone and the paper manual back on its shelf, Snezana took the yard office key from its hook and crossed the yard in the van lights. Nobody on the night counter goes in there. The computer that holds the index hummed behind the door, its screen showing Haverly's job: 7,800 of 12,000 chunks done. Every answer she had read aloud since midnight had come through that room, from an index half in one model's numbers and half in another's. The counter had been fine all night. The cause was across the yard, still working, at 1,500 an hour.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next model change. Questions stay on v1 and ask the old index, 12,000 chunks with v1 numbers. Beside it, a new index is built with v2 at 1,500 chunks an hour. When it is complete, a test set of 5 known questions runs against it and finds 5 of 5 at 08:00. Only then do questions and index switch together.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next model change. Questions stay on v1 and the old index while the new index is built beside it with v2, 1,500 chunks an hour. When the new index is complete, the test set runs against it; at 08:00 it finds 5 of 5 right pages, and only then do questions and index switch together, in one step.

fix.title: The fix: build beside, test, switch together, and label every chunk with its model
fix.text: For every model change, build a second index beside the live one, making every chunk's numbers with the new model, while questions stay on the old model and the old index. When the new index is complete, run a test set of known questions, each with the page that should answer it, against the new index. Switch questions and index together, in one step, only when the test set passes. Keep the old index for a while after the switch, so going back is one step too. Store the name of the model that made each chunk's numbers beside the chunk, and have the search refuse to compare a question with a chunk from another model, so any mix fails loudly with no answer instead of quietly with a wrong one. Start well before the provider's retirement date, so there is time to fix a failing test.

limits: Two indexes for a night means room for both: 12,000 extra lists of numbers here, and for a large library a real storage bill. The old index can go once the new one has served for a while without trouble.
A test set only checks the questions it holds. Five known questions catch tonight's mix; a real one needs the questions staff actually ask, kept up to date as manuals are added.
Questions stay on the old model until the switch, so the old model must still be running. Start the move well before the provider's retirement date, not on its last night.

explain.seniorTake: Treat an embedding index as a second database, built from your documents and written in one model's numbers. Anything that changes those numbers, a new model, a new version of the same model, even a new way of cutting chunks, means moving the whole index, and it deserves the care of moving a database: build beside, test against known answers, switch in one step, and keep the old one until you are sure. Label every chunk with the model that made it, so a mix fails loudly. And be wary of scores. A similarity has no units and no meaning outside one model; a high score between two models is not confidence, it is luck.

realWorld.title: pgvector: exact or approximate
realWorld.text: pgvector adds lists of numbers, which it calls vectors, to the Postgres database. Its README says: "By default, pgvector performs exact nearest neighbor search, which provides perfect recall." Recall here is how many of the truly closest chunks the search finds. It goes on: "You can add an index to use approximate nearest neighbor search, which trades some recall for speed."

realWorld.title: pgvector: an approximate index changes results
realWorld.text: The README warns: "Unlike typical indexes, you will see different results for queries after adding an approximate index." That is one more reason to run a test set of known questions after any change to how the index searches, not only after a model change.

realWorld.title: pgvector: HNSW and IVFFlat
realWorld.text: The README names two kinds of approximate index. "An HNSW index creates a multilayer graph." And: "An IVFFlat index divides vectors into lists, and then searches a subset of those lists that are closest to the query vector." Both are built from one model's numbers, so a new model means building them again.

realWorld.title: pgvector: one length per index
realWorld.text: The README says: "However, you can only create indexes on rows with the same number of dimensions". Dimensions are how many numbers are in each list. v1 and v2 made lists of the same length, so a check like this passes, and nothing in the database can tell one model's numbers from another's. Only a label on each chunk can.

realWorld.title: Malkov and Yashunin, 2016: HNSW
realWorld.text: The paper behind HNSW begins: "We present a new approach for the approximate K-nearest neighbor search". It says "Hierarchical NSW incrementally builds a multi-layer structure consisting from hierarchical set of proximity graphs", and that searching from the top layer "allows a logarithmic complexity scaling": roughly, doubling the chunks adds only a little search time.

asked: Design a RAG system for internal documents.
How do you change the embedding model without downtime?
How do you measure retrieval quality?
interview.answer: I'd build it in two halves. Indexing: cut the documents into chunks, a few to a page, along headings where possible; turn each chunk into an embedding with one embedding model; store each embedding with its chunk, its source page and the model's name in a vector database, with an approximate index such as HNSW once exact search gets slow. Answering: embed the question with the same model, take the closest chunks above a match bar, and hand them to the language model with an instruction to answer only from them and cite the page. The index is a second store that must move with its model, so to change the model without downtime I'd build a new index beside the old one while questions stay on the old model, test it, and switch questions and index together in one step, keeping the old index for a quick way back. The search refuses to compare a question with chunks from another model. To measure retrieval quality I'd keep a test set of real questions, each with the pages that should answer it, and score how often the right page comes back near the top, before every switch and after any change to chunking, the model or the index. I'd tell the story of a tool-hire depot whose re-index ran in place with questions already on the new model: at 04:48 a question about a saw got the cement mixer's page at 0.91, because 4,800 chunks still held the old model's numbers.

terms.def: A business that rents out tools and machines, such as saws, mixers and generators, to builders by the day.
The person behind a depot's counter who hands out tools and answers customers. Snezana works the night counter.
A builder who digs and prepares the ground before building, such as foundations and drains. Grzegorz is one.
A hand-held power saw for cutting concrete, stone and metal. The depot's item C-27 is a petrol one.
A machine with a turning drum that mixes cement, sand and water. The depot's item M-06.
A set of instructions a computer follows. The assistant, the embedding model, the language model and the job are all programs.
The program on the depot's counter that answers questions typed in plain words, from the depot's 3,000 pages of tool manuals.
One short piece of a document, cut so it can be stored and found on its own. The depot's manuals make 12,000, four to a page.
Cutting documents into chunks before they are stored. How the cuts fall decides what each chunk's numbers describe.
A program that turns a piece of text into a long list of numbers, so that texts about similar things get nearby numbers. The depot used v1, then v2.
The list of numbers an embedding model makes for one piece of text, like map co-ordinates for its meaning. Only comparable with embeddings from the same model.
Another name for a list of numbers, such as an embedding. pgvector stores vectors in a database.
All the chunks' embeddings, each kept with its chunk, so the closest ones to a question can be found. A second store, written in one model's numbers.
A store built to keep lists of numbers and find the ones closest to a given list quickly. The depot's index lives in one.
A program that writes text. In the assistant it writes the answer from the chunks it is handed, and can only be as right as those chunks.
Short for retrieval-augmented generation: look the answer up in your own documents, then have a language model write it from what was found.
A score from 0 to 1 for how close two lists of numbers sit. It means something only when both lists come from the same model.
The lowest similarity a chunk must beat to be handed to the language model. 0.80 at the depot.
The company that runs the embedding model for the depot, over the internet. It retires v1 at the end of 30 September.
When a provider stops running an old model, so anything that still uses it stops working.
A program that runs on its own, without anyone typing into it. Haverly's job re-made the chunks' numbers from 00:00.
Making every chunk's numbers again, usually with a new model. Done in place, it writes over the old numbers one chunk at a time.
Changing the one live index chunk by chunk, so that while the job runs, part of it is old and part new.
Making a complete second index next to the live one, while questions keep using the live one, then switching.
Known questions, each with the page that should answer it, run against an index to check it before anyone relies on it.
Moving questions to the new model and the new index in one step, so they are never on different models.
A rule in the search that refuses to compare a question with a chunk whose numbers came from a different model. It needs the model's name stored with every chunk.
A similarity between lists from two different models. It measures nothing, so it can land anywhere, high or low.
Switched off for users. In the warn option, the assistant gives no answers while the job runs.
Time when a system gives users nothing at all, like the 8 hours of the warn option.
The locked office across the depot's yard, where the computer holding the index sits.
The company's central office, where Haverly looks after the assistant and its index.
PostgreSQL, a widely used free database that stores data in tables.
An open-source add-on for Postgres that stores vectors and finds the nearest ones to a query.
Finding the stored lists of numbers closest to a given one. Exact search checks them all; approximate search checks fewer, faster.
How many of the truly closest items a search actually finds. Exact search finds all of them; an approximate index trades some away for speed.
A structure that finds close lists of numbers fast by checking only some of them, so it can miss a few. HNSW and IVFFlat are two kinds.
Short for hierarchical navigable small world: an approximate index built as layers of links between nearby lists, searched from the top layer down.
An approximate index in pgvector that sorts vectors into lists and searches only the lists closest to the query.
How many numbers are in each list. v1 and v2 make lists of the same length, so nothing complained when they were mixed.
Points joined by links. HNSW links each list of numbers to some of its nearest neighbours.
Growing very slowly: each doubling of the items adds only about one more step of search work.
The thing a search is asked to match; here, the question's list of numbers.
An international standard for running information security. Companies can be certified against it.
The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control that expects changes to systems to be planned, assessed, tested and documented.
A voluntary framework from NIST, released on 26 January 2023, for managing the risks of AI systems.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology.
Short for artificial intelligence: programs that do things people would call thinking, such as writing answers.
An international standard for running a management system for artificial intelligence.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud: computers and services rented over the internet.

atWork: Find every place your company searches its own documents by meaning: a help bot, a search box, an assistant over policies. For each, ask four questions. Which embedding model made the stored lists, and is that model's name stored with every chunk? When does the provider say that model retires? Is there a written plan to move the index: build beside, run a test set of known questions with their right pages, and switch questions and index together in one step? Does the search refuse to compare lists from two models? If you use pgvector in Postgres, a column for the model's name next to the embedding is one line of the table's design; on AWS, Amazon's cloud, the same holds for whichever store keeps the vectors. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.32 (change management) is the one an auditor would read a model switch against; ISMS.online's explainer says "The details of these changes must be explicitly stated and documented." A planned re-index with a test set and a recorded switch is that evidence; an in-place job that moved questions at midnight is not. AI systems may also be mapped to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, if your company is pursuing them. Build the model label and the test set into the first design rather than adding them at audit time. This is not audit advice.

recall.prompt: Your company's help bot answers from 50,000 help articles, cut into chunks and stored as embeddings. Last night a scheduled job began re-embedding the chunks with the provider's newer embedding model, and the bot's questions moved to the newer model when the job started. This morning, halfway through, the bot cites an article about printer drivers, with a high similarity, to a question about refunds. What went wrong, and how should the next model change run?

keyIdeas.idea: Questions on the new model were compared with chunks still holding the old model's numbers; a score across two models is chance
Build the new index beside the old, keep questions on the old model until it is complete and passes a test set, then switch both together
Store the model version with every chunk and refuse comparisons across models

recall.model: The bot was comparing two models' numbers. Its questions were embedded by the new model, but half the chunks still held the old model's numbers, and a similarity between two models is chance, so the printer article scored high by luck. Next time, build the new index beside the old one and keep questions on the old model until every chunk is done and a test set of known questions finds its right articles; then switch questions and index together in one step. Store the model version with every chunk, and have the search refuse any comparison where the question's model and the chunk's differ.

recall.prompt: In the sim, replaying 30 September in place, how many chunks hold v2 numbers at 04:48, and what does the C-27 question get?
options: 4,800 on v2; the saw's fuel page at 0.42
7,200 on v2; the cement mixer's drum-speed page at 0.91
7,200 on v2; the saw's fuel page at 0.89
12,000 on v2; the generator's fuel tank page at 0.74
recall.why: From 00:00 the job re-makes 1,500 chunks an hour in chunk order, so at 04:48, 4.8 hours in, chunks 1 to 7,200 hold v2 numbers and 4,800 still hold v1's. The saw's chunk 9,612 and the mixer's 11,208 are both still v1, so the v2 question meets them as chance scores: 0.42 for the saw, 0.91 for the mixer, and the mixer is handed over.

recall.prompt: Why doesn't raising the match bar from 0.80 to 0.95 fix an in-place re-index?
options: It does: no wrong page can score above 0.95
Scores between two models are chance, so a wrong page can still pass, and right pages on one model score below 0.95
0.95 is still too low; the bar should be 0.99
The bar applies only to the language model, not to the index
recall.why: A similarity between a v2 question and v1 numbers measures nothing, so it can land anywhere: in the sim the saw's carry case page scores 0.97 for the trimmer question. Meanwhile right pages on one model score 0.84 to 0.89, so after 08:00 the 0.95 bar refuses all of them: 0 of 5.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how do you change the embedding model behind a RAG system without downtime, and how do you know the new index is good?

keyIdeas.idea: Build a second index beside the live one while questions stay on the old model and old index
Run a test set of known questions with their right pages against the new index before switching
Switch questions and index together in one step, and store the model version with every chunk

recall.model: The index is a second store written in one model's numbers, so it has to move with the model. I'd build a second index beside the live one, making every chunk's numbers with the new model, while questions stay on the old model and the old index. When it is complete I'd run a test set of known questions, each with its right pages, against the new index, and score how often the right page comes back near the top. Only if it passes would I switch questions and index together in one step, keeping the old index for a quick way back. And I'd store the model version with every chunk, so the search refuses to compare a question with a chunk from another model.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. We moved to v3 on the night of Monday 29 March, the new way: a second index built beside the old one from 00:00, questions on v2 until the test set passed, and every chunk labelled with its model. At 08:00 the test set found all 5 right pages, and questions and index switched together. Then at 09:10 a customer asked about our new stump grinder, R-50. Haverly had added its manual at 03:00 that night: 40 pages, 160 chunks. The assistant said it had no matching pages. The old index had them. The new one didn't.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. The new index passed its test set. Why can't it find the grinder, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Chunks added during the build went only into the old index; the new index was built from the chunks as they stood at 00:00
Write every new or changed chunk to both indexes during the build, or run a catch-up pass before the switch
Check before switching: compare the chunk counts, and keep the test set current with the newest items

coldCase.model: The new index was built from the chunks as they stood at 00:00. Haverly added the grinder's 160 chunks at 03:00, during the build, and they went only into the old index, which questions were still using, so nobody noticed; the new index never saw them, and the test set had no grinder question to catch it. Changes made while a new index builds must reach it: write every new or changed chunk to both indexes until the switch, or run a catch-up pass before the switch that embeds whatever changed since the build began. Then check before switching: compare the chunk counts of the two indexes, 12,160 against 12,000, and keep the test set current, with a question for the newest item on the shelves.
